prompt: Which of the following National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) standards provides a Code for High Power Rocketry?
explanation: NFPA 1127 is the Code for High Power Rocketry. NFPA 1122 covers Model Rocketry; NFPA 1124 covers Manufacture, Transportation, and Storage of Fireworks; NFPA 1125 covers Manufacture of Model and High Power Rocket Motors.

prompt: What part of the Federal Aviation Regulations govern rocket activity?
explanation: Rocket activity is codified in Part 101 — Moored Balloons, Kites, Amateur Rockets, Unmanned Free Balloons, and Certain Model Aircraft.

prompt: What is the maximum launch (flight-ready) weight allowable for a rocket which does not require an FAA Certificate of Waiver or Authorization (COA)?
explanation: Per Part 101.22(5), flight-ready rockets weighing no more than 1,500 grams (53 oz or 3.3 lbs) are defined as Class 1-Model Rockets. Class 1 rockets do not require a COA.

prompt: What is the maximum propellant weight allowable for a rocket which does not require an FAA Certificate of Waiver or Authorization (COA)?
explanation: Per Part 101.22(1), rockets using no more than 125 g (4.4 oz) are defined as Class 1-Model Rockets. Class 1 rockets do not require a COA.

prompt: Which of the following is a requirement for High Power Rocket Motor User Certification (excludes NAR Jr. HPR Participation Program)?

options.text: The ability to understand written English instructions
A minimum of 18 years of age
A citizen of the United States of America

explanation: A minimum of 18 years of age.

prompt: What is the maximum total impulse permitted in a High Power Rocket per NFPA 1127?

options.text: There is no impulse limit provided the altitude requirements listed in the FAA Certificate of Waiver or Authorization (COA) are not exceeded

explanation: 40,960 Newton-seconds.

prompt: What is the maximum allowable weight for a High Power Rocket permitted per NFPA 1127?

options.text: There is no limit provided the rocket weighs less than 1/3 of the average certified thrust of the motors intended to be ignited at launch

explanation: There is no limit provided the rocket weighs less than 1/3 of the average certified thrust of the motors intended to ignite at launch.

prompt: What is the minimum age for User Certification (excludes NAR Jr. HPR Participation Program)?
explanation: 18 years old.

prompt: Which of the following characteristics does NOT meet the definition of a High Power Rocket motor?

options.text: Total impulse is more than 160 Newton-seconds

explanation: Propellant type is not a defining characteristic.

prompt: Which of the following is (are) true of a complex High Power Rocket per NFPA 1127?

options.text: The rocket is multi-staged or propelled by a cluster of rocket motors
The rocket contains electrical or electronic devices intended for control of the rocket's functions (e.g. staging, recovery initiation, etc.)
The rocket uses other than parachute or streamer recovery (e.g. helicopter, glide recovery, etc.)

explanation: Multi-staged or propelled by a cluster of rocket motors.

prompt: According to NFPA 1127, a launch site is defined as containing areas for which of the following activities?
explanation: All of the above.

prompt: A person shall fly a High Power Rocket only in compliance with:

options.text: Federal, state, and local laws, rules, regulations, statutes, and ordinances

explanation: All of the above.

prompt: According to NFPA 1127, which of the following statements is always true concerning the definition of a hybrid rocket motor?

options.text: The fuel component is composed of either paper or plastic
The fuel is in a different physical state (solid, liquid, or gaseous) than the oxidizer
The oxidizer component is nitrous oxide

explanation: The fuel and oxidizer are in different physical states.

prompt: You're attending a launch that has a thin (but see-through) cloud layer at ~3,000 feet and clear blue skies above it. Is it okay to "punch" through this cloud layer with a High Power Rocket if there's a Certificate of Waiver or Authorization (COA) granting Class 2 flights up to 6,000 feet?

options.text: Yes, since there is an active COA, High Power Rockets can be flown up to the 6,000 foot altitude limit
No, flights into any clouds are prohibited unless specifically waived by the FAA
Yes, as long as the cloud layer can barely be seen through and the RSO allows it

explanation: Part 101.25 specifically states that you must not operate Class 2-High Power Rockets into any cloud. Flights into clouds are not permitted regardless of opacity.

prompt: You are attending a launch where the sky is almost completely obscured by clouds at 5,000 feet except for a ~1,000 foot wide "hole" directly over the launch pads. Is it okay to launch a High Power Rocket to 6,000 feet if there's a Certificate of Waiver or Authorization (COA) granting Class 2 flights up to 8,000 feet?

options.text: Yes, as long as the High Power Rocket stays within the cloud opening
Yes, as long as the RSO approves the launch and the COA is active
No, the five-tenths coverage and horizontal visibility limitations apply

explanation: Part 101.25 prohibits operation at any altitude where more than 50% of the sky is cloud-covered or where horizontal visibility is less than five miles, unless the FAA has waived these. The hole must be at least 10 miles wide for compliance.

prompt: According to NFPA 1127, which one of the following statements is true concerning the definition of a High Power Rocket motor?

options.text: Total impulse is less than 81,920 Newton-seconds
The total impulse is more than 160 Newton-seconds
The motor must use either fiberglass or metal case materials

explanation: Total impulse more than 160 N-s is one of the qualifying conditions for a high-power motor.

prompt: Which of the following (hypothetical) rocket motors is NOT a High Power Rocket motor?

options.text: An F90 with 40 grams of propellant
An H60 with 62 grams of propellant
A G35 with 66 grams of propellant
All of the above are High Power Rocket motors

explanation: A HPR motor must have more than 160 N-s total impulse, OR avg thrust > 80 N, OR more than 125 g of propellant. The F90 has >80 N avg thrust; the H60 has >160 N-s; the G35 does not exceed any threshold.

prompt: What information does FAA FAR 101.29(a) require you to provide when filing for FAA Launch Authorization?

options.text: Estimated number of rockets and type of propulsion (liquid or solid), fuel(s) and oxidizer(s)
Description of the launcher(s) planned to be used, including any airborne platform(s) and description of recovery system
Highest altitude, above ground level, expected to be reached, launch site latitude, longitude, and elevation, and any additional safety procedures that will be followed

explanation: All of the above are required.

prompt: Which of the following are operating limitations for Class 2 High Power Rockets per the FAA's FAR 101 Regulations?

options.text: At any altitude where clouds or obscuring phenomena of more than five-tenths coverage prevails
At any altitude where the horizontal visibility is less than five miles

explanation: All of the above are operating limitations under FAR Part 101.25.

prompt: According to NFPA 1127, a High Power Rocket shall only be launched if:

options.text: It contains any combination of motors having 40,960 Newton-seconds of total impulse or less
It contains a recovery system that is designed to return all parts to the ground intact and at a landing speed at which the rocket does not present a hazard
It utilizes an electronically actuated recovery system as either a primary or backup deployment method if the installed total impulse is greater than 2560 Newton-seconds

explanation: All of the above are required.

prompt: According to NFPA 1127, when is it acceptable to alter a High Power Rocket motor?

options.text: When the results of a simulation show that a different delay time is needed for optimal deployment
When the motor manufacturer allows it
It is never acceptable to modify a High Power Rocket motor

explanation: When the motor manufacturer allows it. Motor delay times should only be adjusted using procedures provided by the motor manufacturer.

prompt: According to NFPA 1127, the definition of a High Power Rocket is a rocket vehicle that:

options.text: Is propelled by one or more High Power Rocket motors

Is propelled by a combination of model rocket motors having an installed total impulse of more than 320 Newton-seconds or a combination of model rocket motors having more than a total of 125 grams (4.4 ounces) of propellant weight
Weighs more than 1500 grams (53 ounces or 3.3 pounds) with motor(s) installed

explanation: All of the above.
